{{short description|Ancient Greek mathematician}}

'''Leon''' ({{langx|el|Λέων}}) was a Greek [[mathematician]] and pupil of [[Neocleides]].<ref>{{citation|title=A Short History of Greek Mathematics|first=James|last=Gow|publisher=University Press|year=1884|page=183|quote=Of Neocleides and his pupil Leon also, we know no more than the Eudemian summary tells us, in which the only important fact is that Leon wrote an improved 'Elements' and treated particularly of diorismus.|url=https://archive.org/details/ashorthistorygr00gowgoog}}</ref> Leon was active from around 370 to 340 BCE.<ref>''A New History of Greek Mathematics'', Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2022, {{ISBN|978-1-108-83384-4}}.</ref> His book ''Elements'' was overshadowed by [[Euclid]]'s [[Euclid's Elements|work of the same name]].

[[Proclus]] states the following<ref>[[Thomas Taylor (neoplatonist)|Thomas Taylor]], ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=2SBeEnT45gsC The Philosophical and Mathematical Commentaries of Proclus on the First Book of Euclid's Elements]'' Vol. 1 (1788)</ref> in his ''Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements'':<blockquote>But Neoclides was junior to [[Leodamas of Thasos|Leodamas]], and his disciple was Leon; who added many things to those thought of by former geometricians. So that Leon also constructed elements more accurate, both on account of their multitude, and on account of the use which they exhibit: and besides this, he discovered a method of determining when a problem, whose investigation is sought for, is possible, and when it is impossible.</blockquote>
